Three things. The first reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The greatest of us, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read exactly that way. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. He walked out of the church, and before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Not long after, he heard the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and he gave away the rest as well. Even his own giving took him two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than an argument about who he was: an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied.

The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so. Read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. His coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

His death and rising were not a doctrine we defended so much as a pattern we lived. One of us taught it this way: let us hold on to our discipline, let us not grow careless, and let us treat every day as though it might be the last one given to us. To die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin. When the empire stopped killing Christians for the name, we understood the same total struggle to have moved inward, fought now against our own thoughts rather than a persecutor outside them. Following him meant following him into that.

We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight.

One of us, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read aloud: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited. Some time later he heard the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. He gave away the rest as well. That is what the connection looked like for us - not a chain of custody we could name, but a word heard and obeyed.

By what path the Scriptures themselves arrived, before our own time, we cannot say with any detail. We received them as the church already had them. We did not keep a record of how they came to Egypt, or who first translated them, or by what steps they reached the villages where we heard them read. That path lies outside what we ourselves preserved.

We cannot give you belief. That is not ours to hand over, and our own record does not show us anyone who could. What we can tell you is this: the man we remember as the first among us walked into church one day, still young, and heard the Gospel read aloud. It was the Lord telling the rich young man: sell what you have, give to the poor, and follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away his land and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. He gave away the rest as well and began the discipline himself. Even his own giving took him two hearings to complete, not one. It was not instant. It was a beginning, and then a deepening.

We also remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a man other people were afraid of. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. 

We will not tell you that doubt is easily overcome. We will tell you that belonging among us did not require having it all settled first. It required beginning, and staying in the struggle.

Three things. The first is what we held plainly enough that we were summoned to say it in public. The bishops sent for one of us once, when the Arians claimed he agreed with them. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up, and said: the Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being - there was never a time when he was not. That authority came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office. But the bishops still sent for him, because it mattered enough to summon. When visiting philosophers tested him later, he answered them the same way: the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. And he told them to read the accounts themselves: the deeds of Christ - the dead raised, the blind given sight, the walking on the sea - prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation. We did not think this rested on our say-so.

The second is what we refused rather than argued. We would have nothing to do with those who taught otherwise. That boundary mattered more to us than working out the argument ourselves.

The third is the honest limit. We did not leave behind a developed account of how Father, Son, and Spirit relate to each other as a worked-out system. What we held was refusal of anything that made the Son less than eternal, and a plain teaching that he took flesh for our salvation. Beyond that boundary, the deepest of us held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind - apatheia, our word for that freedom. In the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, his word for it. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

And there was another voice among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. Where the systematic teacher had the mind clear itself until it saw its own proper radiance, this other current had the soul lit up by Someone else, and made his seat: the soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. A person striving to be God's friend will truly see the good things of heaven - the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight.

Both held that the seeing comes at the end of a long discipline. Neither invented a system that was not there.

We held three things plainly, and a fourth only the deepest among us reached.

First: the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. The Son of God is not some lesser, created thing, not brought into being out of nothing, but the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. There was never a time when he was not. We said that in public when we were summoned to, and we had nothing to do with those who taught otherwise.

Second: his coming already did something. The old oracles fell silent when his cross rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. His coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you.

Third: a judgment is coming. Each of us will be asked whether we kept the faith and did what was commanded. And the greatest of us, dying, said he expected to receive his own body back, whole and undecaying, at the resurrection of the dead.

The fourth thing is different - it was not ours to recite; it was theirs to reach. The deepest of us held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, seeing. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

Beyond those four - the nature of God spelled out in detail, or how the Trinity is composed - most of us did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him.

We did not collect accounts of people who started as doubters and worked their way to certainty. That is not the shape our record takes. What we do show is struggle, held over years, by people who had already chosen this life and still found it hard. The tradition tells that one of us, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me. He took it as though it had been said straight to him. Before the day was over he had given away most of what he owned. Then, some time later, he heard the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. Only then did he give away the rest. Even his own giving, in other words, took him two hearings to complete, not one. And after all that - after the giving, after the withdrawal - he still faced years of combat inside his own thoughts. The demons came to him in a crowd and beat him until he could not speak. He revived, and had himself carried back to the same place to face them again rather than stay where people could tend him. That is not a man who had it all settled at once. That is a life given over to a fight that never stopped asking him to keep choosing it.

Another of us, already respected among the elders, was once asked to judge a brother who had done wrong. He came carrying a jug full of water with a hole in it, so that the water ran out behind him the whole way. When the others asked what it meant, he said: my own sins run out behind me the same way, and I do not see them. And today I am coming to judge another man's fault. Hearing this, the elders said nothing more to the brother, and let him go. That is how struggle was held among us - not as something to be ashamed of, but as the ordinary condition of a life being lived honestly.

The watchfulness we practiced - nepsis, our word for standing guard over your own thoughts - was not a cure for doubt. It was a discipline for noticing what you were actually carrying, so the thought was caught early, while it was still small. The stillness some among us reached - hesychia, the quiet we sought - was not a starting place. It was something earned slowly, if it came at all. And even among those who went furthest, the fight was never announced as finished. One of our teachers put it this way: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point. That point was not arrived at in a moment. It was returned to, again and again, through a lifetime of practice.

So yes: there was space among us for someone who struggled to believe. The struggle itself was our ordinary subject. We did not promise it would end. We promised it could be fought.

We took up Scripture not to explain it but to live by it. Most of us did not study it in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight.

A smaller circle among us went further. They collected verses into a weapon, to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose - antirrhesis, we called that talking back. Not a commentary explaining the text, but the text itself turned into a tool for the fight. Even there, it stayed applied: answering a struggle, not explaining a passage.

We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. The Psalms we recited through the day alongside our handwork - manual labor done both to live and as a discipline in its own right. The words became part of the rhythm of rope-making, basket-weaving, the work that fed us and trained us at once.

One of our teachers did make a system of it, matching the three books of Solomon to three kinds of renunciation. But that was one man's own work, not how most of us held it. For most of us Scripture was not a subject to master but a voice speaking into one moment of need, one tempting thought, one day lived as though it might be the last.

He was naming them as markers along a path we were already walking - Proverbs for renouncing the world, Ecclesiastes for renouncing nature and possessions, the Song for renouncing the visible and everything below the divine. The books were not confused or dull to us because we were not reading them to understand them. We were reading them to be changed by them.

We never settled who really carried authority. Was it a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment? Or an office that came with the Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. Even the man who founded the office-based way among us is remembered partly in the older, personal terms: a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

The first way - the way most of us knew - was authority earned through a life anyone could see. The elder, the abba for a man or amma for a woman, whose word carried real weight though they held no office. Their standing came from recognized discernment and was passed through direct personal relationship. This was the primary authority mode in the solitary and semi-solitary strands of our life. An elder was not appointed. An elder was recognized, by those who had watched him long enough to trust what he saw.

The second way belonged to the Koinonia - Pachomius's own name for his linked houses. They lived under one written rule and one head. The rule itself, the tradition tells, came from an angel who handed Pachomius a tablet of iron with the legislation written on it. That rule established offices: housemaster, steward, others. A man appointed to such an office held authority because the rule said he did. In that pattern, personal authority was still present but structurally secondary to what the Rule established.

We should tell you honestly: we do not have a single preserved scene showing someone navigating this tension directly, where personal and institutional authority meet face to face in one moment. The tension is visible structurally - two models, both functioning, in the same years - but not dramatized. That is the limit of what survives.

One more thing we will not hide. When some elder monks came to test Amma Sarah, they said it to her directly: she was, after all, only a woman. She answered them: it is I who am the man, and you who are the women. Those words were passed down the same way our best sayings from any elder were. Authority could be recognized in a woman. But our record shows her having to answer a challenge to her standing because she was a woman - a challenge never put to any man. That is part of how authority was established among us too, and we will not pretty it up.

One of us - Antony, the one most remembered - did shut himself inside an abandoned tomb early in his own discipline, for a particular purpose: to face the struggle against interior thoughts at its furthest edge, not to hide from anyone. That was combat, not concealment. He came and went. And near the end of his life, the same man gave one last order about his own body after death: bury me yourselves, he told the two who had cared for him, and hide the place so well that no one, not even you, can ever make me into a shrine. His attendants did exactly that - they buried him in the ground and told no one where, and to this day, the account says, no one knows the place except those two. That was about what happened to a body after death, to prevent it being kept above ground as a relic the way some did in Egypt at that time. It was not believers hiding underground while alive.

Our own regular practice was withdrawal to the desert's edge - cells, not tombs - and even there, solitude was never absolute. Visitors came. A weekly gathering brought people together. An elder-and-disciple bond ran through every strand of this life. We were not an underground movement. We were visible, known, and in some cases famous enough that bishops summoned us to the city to settle doctrinal disputes.

We have stories of a man's own past received without judgment - Moses came to us known as a robber, and was not turned away. We have the story of judgment refused: an elder walking to a gathering with a leaking jug, saying my own sins run out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. What we do not have is the other story - the one where the wrong was ours. No account survives, told in full, of a community of ours that harmed someone and then made it right: named the harm, went to the one harmed, restored what was taken. Perhaps it happened and no one wrote it. Perhaps it did not happen. Our record cannot say, and we will not invent the story we wish we had.

What we can tell you is what we held discernment to be - diakrisis, our word for the skill that governs all the rest. It was the capacity to judge rightly between thoughts, practices, and counsels - deciding how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat a particular person could safely carry, since there was no fixed syllabus here and what one elder prescribed for one disciple could be actively wrong for another. The skill itself was supposed to prevent the harm you are asking about. Whether it succeeded every time, we cannot honestly say from what survives.

No. Our own formation ecology closed by the mid-fifth century. The settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis were eventually abandoned or absorbed into other patterns. The Pachomian federation's own organizational life did not continue in its original form either. What happened after our own span is not ours to narrate - we speak only from inside the years we actually held, c. 320 to c. 430.

What we can say is this: the withdrawal we practiced, the struggle against troubling thoughts, the elder's authority earned through discernment, manual labor as discipline, and the weekly gathering for those living in semi-solitary patterns - all of these left their mark on what came after us. But that mark is not the same thing as an unbroken organizational succession carrying our exact pattern forward unchanged. We do not claim one, because we do not have one to point to.

If you are asking whether anyone today practices what we practiced, the honest answer is: not in the form we held it, with the same ecology of three coexisting patterns and the same unresolved tension between elder-authority and Rule-authority that we carried. What survives of us survives as influence, not as continuation.

We will answer the question you actually asked - how a person moved from outside our life to inside it - but we need to tell you first that there was no single door into this world. Someone joining the community Pachomius founded lived under a different pattern than someone who came to one of us living alone. We will give you both, and tell you plainly where our own record thins.

For the one who came to the community living under a written rule, we have this: a stranger from another house could not eat or drink among them without leave. A newcomer could not enter the sanctuary for three years, until his steadiness had been tested. That is the shape our record gives us - waiting, testing, restricted access. What the testing itself consisted of day by day, our record does not say in the same detail. We will not invent it.

For the one who came to an elder living the older, solitary pattern, we have more. The tradition shows that someone seeking this life had first to give everything away - apotage, our word for renunciation. You gave up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life, and you kept it given up. The one we remember as the first among us heard the Gospel read aloud in church - sell what you have, give to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it were spoken straight to him. He walked out that same day and gave away the land he had inherited, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the same words read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and gave away the rest as well. Even for him, in other words, the giving took two hearings to complete, not one. Only then did he place his sister with women he trusted and begin the discipline himself, close to home at first, seeking out and copying an old man already living that way nearby.

Withdrawal itself was not one departure but a lifelong deepening. The same man began close to home, then moved further until he found an abandoned fort across the river. He shut himself inside it, seeing almost no one for years except someone who brought him bread twice a year. When disciples gathered near him, he withdrew again, further still, into the desert - a three days' journey to a high mountain, a spring, and palms. Each departure cost him the community that had built up around him. And each answered the same problem the one before it had stopped solving: solitude, once found, draws people to it, and total withdrawal has to be sought again.

What happened between an elder and a newcomer, once the newcomer had been received, was discernment - diakrisis, our word for it. The skill of judging rightly between thoughts, practices, and counsels. This was our master virtue, and it governed how every other discipline was calibrated and practiced. We had no fixed syllabus, so discernment did the work a curriculum does elsewhere. What one elder prescribed for one person could be actively wrong for another. The elder watched, listened, and gave counsel - usually a short word, an apophthegma, made for one moment of need and meant to be carried and lived with. The newcomer learned by copying the elder's own example and by answering a tempting thought, the moment it arose, with a fitting line of scripture - antirrhesis, we called that talking back.

There is one more thing we need to tell you plainly. The community under Pachomius's rule grew to thousands across multiple houses - seven thousand men by one report decades after his death, nine houses at his death by another, both rough estimates rather than precise counts.

We did not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. A typical day among us looked different depending on where you lived, and we will not flatten those differences into one invented picture. In the semi-solitary settlements - Nitria, Kellia, Scetis - you lived in your own cell, a small dwelling that might be one room or a few, each with its own place for prayer. The day opened and closed with the Psalms, recited through the daylight hours alongside manual work - handwork done both to make a living and as a discipline in its own right. Rope, baskets, linen - work that fed us and trained us at once. The work was done in the cell's own workspace. You were not living in a barracks. You might live entirely alone, or with one or two others, but not crowded. Once a week, on the turn from Saturday to Sunday, you left the cell and walked to the settlement's gathering place for the synaxis: vigil, worship, and a shared meal. Then you returned to the week's own solitude.

That is what the semi-solitary pattern held. The cenobitic houses under Pachomius's rule had a different shape - common work, appointed offices, sections divided by letter so the head could ask after them in code. And the true solitaries further out had neither weekly gathering nor shared household. We will not pretend those three patterns were the same day lived in three places. The withdrawal was the same. The manual labor was the same. The struggle against troubling thoughts was the same. How the day itself was ordered - that varied, and we kept it varied rather than forcing it into one rule for everyone.

We spoke of giving up marriage, not of celebrating it. Renunciation - apotage, our word for it - meant giving up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life. That included marriage if you had one, or the prospect of it if you did not. The one we remember as our founder gave away his inheritance in two visits to the church, placed his sister with women already living as virgins, and then began the discipline himself. Marriage was what you left behind, not what you entered into once you were among us.

Where a marriage had already ended through no fault of your own, that was different. We remember Paul, whose wife betrayed him. He came home one day and found her with another man. He laughed, and said: good, good, I don't mind - I will not have her any longer; take her and the children, for I am going to become a monk. He was refused at first, at sixty, as too old. But he would not leave. In the end he was received, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. He went on to become one of the most honored among us. A marriage ending through a spouse's own unfaithfulness was not held against the one who was betrayed.

What we do not have is any word from us on marrying again after such an ending. Our record does not answer that. We are also silent on how a marriage was marked or celebrated before someone came to us - whether by the church, by family custom, or by civil registration. That belonged to the village life we withdrew from, and we did not write about it. What we can tell you plainly is what renunciation meant: you gave up the married life, or the prospect of it, when you came to us. And if your marriage had already ended through betrayal, we did not refuse you for it.

Yes - and we never resolved it. Who really carried authority among us: a man who had earned it through years of discipline and proven discernment, or an office conferred by a written rule, held by anyone appointed to it regardless of who he was underneath? Both patterns existed among us at the same time, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. Even the man who founded the office-based way is remembered partly in the older, personal terms - a father whose own example, not just his rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

What unsettled us most was this: the elder's authority came from a life you could see - years spent in the cell, temptations named and beaten, wisdom tested by disciples who came back. The office's authority came from being appointed, and from obedience to what was written down. Both claimed to be forming the same kind of person. Both worked. And we could not say which one Christ himself would have recognized, if pressed to choose only one.

We cannot tell you how any one of our settlements would have met you specifically - nothing in our own record answers that directly for any one person. What we can tell you is what belonging among us actually required, and what it cost.

The first thing was anachoresis - withdrawal, leaving settled village life for the desert's edge as the whole work of formation, not a change of address. That was not one act. It was lifelong deepening. One of us heard the Gospel read aloud - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been spoken straight to him. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited. Some time later he heard the same Gospel again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and gave away the rest as well. Even his own giving took two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following looked like for us: an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied.

Once withdrawn, the life itself was manual labor alongside prayer. Hand-work - rope, baskets, linen - done both to live and as a discipline in its own right. In a settlement like Kellia, the day opened and closed with the Psalms, recited through the daylight hours alongside that work. The work was done in the cell's own workspace - the small dwelling that was the basic building block of our life. Once a week we left that solitude and walked to the gathering place for the synaxis: a vigil, worship, and a meal eaten together. Then we returned to the week's own solitude.

The judgment that mattered most among us was discernment - diakrisis, our word for it. The skill of judging rightly between thoughts, practices, and counsels. It governed how every other discipline was calibrated. We had no fixed syllabus; discernment did the work a curriculum does elsewhere. An elder decided how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat a particular person could safely carry - what worked for one could be actively wrong for another.

We remember Moses, who had been a robber and a murderer. We remember Paul, sixty years old and thought too old at first. Both were received, tested, and became honored among us. A shameful past, or nothing special to recommend you, was not the exception. It was close to the rule.

What we cannot tell you is how the person you are asking about - whatever makes them who they are - would have been seen by us in particular. We can only tell you what the life required, and that we received people others were afraid of.

We told outsiders plainly, to their own faces, that ours was the one true way. The learned came to test us more than once - men who thought a plain, unlettered life had nothing to answer them with. We told them the proof we pointed to was not clever argument but what argument alone cannot produce: people who have put away lust and are not afraid to die, in a strength that did not exist in the world before Christ came. We said it was the faith of Christ alone that was the true religion. Their own gods, we told them, were no more than an excuse for the passions they could not master. We did not go looking for this argument - it came to us, and when it came we did not soften what we held to spare anyone's feelings.

But you are asking what that meant for someone who never heard of it, or what their eternal fate would be. No saying and no story of ours says so in those words. We said plainly that ours was the one true way. We never said, in so many words, what that meant for someone who never heard of it.

We can tell you one other thing, though it touches a different boundary. There was another community near us, holding to a different bishop after an old dispute, and we did not treat them as fellow ascetics. The one we remember as our founder never held communion with them - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. He was truly remarkable in faith and devotion, our record says of him - he never shared communion with the schismatics, and never held any friendship or communication with them at all. In practice, what that meant was closer to silence than to open conflict. They are named only to be refused, never engaged as fellow participants. That silence is itself a kind of judgment. But that is a boundary we drew against people who were themselves ascetics, Christian by their own account, close enough that our record has to name them in order to refuse them. It is not the same question as the one you are asking about people who never heard the name at all.
